title: Your Doctor Uses a BMI of 25 to Decide Whether to Screen You for Diabetes. For South Asians, the Correct Number Is 20. A Harvard-Led Study Says the Current Threshold Is Missing Millions.
excerpt: A cross-sectional analysis of NHANES data found that a 35-year-old Asian American at BMI 25 already has nearly triple the diabetes prevalence of a White American at the same weight. The screening system was never designed for your body.
body:
The number that determines whether your doctor screens you for diabetes is 25. If your Body Mass Index is 25 kg/m² or above and you are between 35 and 70 years old, the US Preventive Services Task Force says you should be tested. Below 25, you are statistically unlikely to have diabetes, and the screening is not recommended.

That threshold was calibrated on White Americans. And a study published in the *Annals of Internal Medicine* by researchers at Harvard Medical School and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center has now demonstrated, with granular NHANES data, exactly how wrong it is for everyone else — especially South Asians.

## The Core Finding

Using data from NHANES cycles between 2011 and 2018, investigators led by Dr. Rahul Aggarwal and senior author Dr. Dhruv Kazi found that the prevalence of diabetes among 35-year-old Asian Americans at a BMI of 25 is 3.8 percent. For White Americans at the same age and BMI, it is 1.4 percent.

That is nearly triple the risk at the same weight.

To achieve equivalent screening sensitivity — meaning the same probability of catching diabetes that the current threshold catches in White Americans — the BMI cutoff for Asian Americans should be 20 kg/m², with a plausible range extending down to below 18.5 kg/m². For Black Americans, the threshold is below 18.5. For Hispanic Americans, it is 18.5.

"The simplicity of a single screening threshold for all Americans is alluring, but it is deeply inequitable," said Dr. Kazi, associate director of the Smith Center and associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.

## Why This Matters for Indian Americans

South Asians develop type 2 diabetes at lower body weights, younger ages, and higher rates than virtually any other ethnic group in the United States. This is not news to endocrinologists who treat Indian American patients. But the formal screening infrastructure — the guidelines that tell primary care physicians when to order a fasting glucose or HbA1c — has never caught up.

The practical consequence: an Indian American man with a BMI of 22 walks into his annual physical. His doctor, following USPSTF guidelines, does not order a diabetes screening. The patient is told he is healthy. His fasting glucose, had it been tested, would have been 118 mg/dL — solidly in the prediabetes range.

This is not a hypothetical. It is happening in clinics across the country, every day. And by the time these patients are eventually diagnosed — often years later, when symptoms become impossible to ignore — the disease has progressed to a point where complications are far more likely.

## The Biology Behind the Disparity

South Asians carry a disproportionate share of visceral fat — the metabolically active fat that wraps around organs and drives insulin resistance — relative to their total body weight. A South Asian man at BMI 23 may have the same visceral fat load as a White man at BMI 28.

This means BMI, a crude ratio of weight to height, systematically underestimates metabolic risk in South Asian bodies. The number on the scale looks reassuring. The biology underneath is not.

Previous research has documented this at the population level. The Indian Council of Medical Research has long used a BMI of 23 as the threshold for overweight in Indian populations. The WHO has recommended lower BMI cutoffs for Asian populations since 2004. But the American screening system, which governs care for over 5 million Indian Americans, has not adopted these adjustments.

## What You Should Actually Do

**Ask for the test regardless of your BMI.** If you are South Asian and over 30, request a fasting glucose and HbA1c at your next annual physical. You do not need to wait for your BMI to cross 25. Your doctor can order it — the barrier is awareness, not insurance coverage.

**Know your family history in detail.** Among Indian Americans, a first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes is not an anomaly — it is the norm. If either parent developed diabetes before age 60, your screening should start at 25, regardless of weight.

**Do not rely on BMI as a reassurance.** A BMI of 22 in a South Asian body is not metabolically equivalent to a BMI of 22 in a White body. Waist circumference (above 90 cm for South Asian men, 80 cm for women) is a better proxy for visceral fat and metabolic risk than BMI alone.

**Push your physician.** Many primary care doctors are aware of the racial disparities in diabetes risk but continue to follow USPSTF guidelines because they provide medicolegal cover. A polite, informed request for early screening is almost never refused.

## The Systemic Problem

The study's authors are careful to note that fixing screening thresholds is necessary but not sufficient. Structural inequities in healthcare access, insurance coverage, and follow-up care mean that even when diabetes is diagnosed early in minority populations, outcomes remain worse.

But diagnosis is the starting point. And right now, the starting point is calibrated to the wrong population.

"Delayed diagnosis and inadequate treatment of diabetes can produce catastrophic consequences, jeopardising one's heart, kidney, eyes, and limbs," said Dr. Aggarwal. "Making screening more equitable is a place to start."

For the 5.4 million Indian Americans living in the United States, that start is overdue by at least two decades.
author: Diaspora Desk
